candidates.title: Pericapsular Nerve Group Block Significantly Reduces Morphine Consumption and Improves Early Recovery Following Primary Total Hip Arthroplasty: A Randomized Double-Blind Sham-Controlled Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Demirkıran F, Özdemir Kol İ, Altun O
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: The pericapsular nerve group (PENG) block has emerged as a promising regional analgesic technique for hip surgery. However, evidence regarding its opioid-sparing efficacy following primary total hip arthroplasty remains limited. This study evaluated the effect of ultrasound-guided PENG block on postoperative opioid consumption, pain scores, and recovery outcomes following primary total hip arthroplasty. METHODS: In this prospective, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial, 40 patients undergoing elective primary total hip arthroplasty under general anesthesia were randomized to receive either ultrasound-guided PENG block with one mg/kg bupivacaine diluted to 30 mL (n = 20) or a sham procedure with 30 mL saline (n = 20). The primary outcome was cumulative morphine consumption during the first 24 postoperative hours. The secondary outcomes included visual analog scale (VAS) pain scores, time to first rescue analgesia, patient satisfaction, and opioid-related adverse events. Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups. RESULTS: Cumulative morphine consumption was significantly lower in the PENG group throughout the postoperative period and at 24 hours (6.2 ± 3.3 versus 30.2 ± 5.6 mg, P < 0.001), representing an approximately 79% reduction in opioid requirement. The visual analog scale pain scores were significantly lower at all postoperative assessment points (all P < 0.001). Time to first rescue analgesic requirement was significantly prolonged in the PENG group (16.0 ± 0.0 versus 1.4 ± 0.5 hours, P < 0.001). Patient satisfaction was significantly greater in the PENG group (P < 0.001), while postoperative nausea occurred less frequently (zero versus 25%, P = 0.017). There were no block-related complications observed. CONCLUSIONS: Ultrasound-guided PENG block provided effective opioid-sparing analgesia following primary total hip arthroplasty, significantly reducing postoperative morphine consumption and pain scores while improving patient satisfaction and reducing postoperative nausea. These findings support the incorporation of PENG block into multimodal analgesic protocols for total hip arthroplasty.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large database study with immediately actionable findings on SSRI-associated bleeding and infection risk after THA, directly relevant to perioperative medication management with strong clinical implications.
bullets: In adults undergoing primary total hip arthroplasty, a PENG block reduced 24-hour morphine consumption by roughly 79% compared to sham (6.2 mg vs 30.2 mg).
Patients who received the PENG block went about 16 hours before needing rescue analgesia, versus under 2 hours in the control group.
For primary total hip arthroplasty patients, adding a PENG block to multimodal analgesia meaningfully cuts opioid use, lowers pain scores, and reduces postoperative nausea.

candidates.title: Adalimumab Does Not Improve Clinical Outcomes After Needle Fasciotomy for Dupuytren Contracture: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Brouwers J, Claessens F, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Dupuytren disease is a fibroproliferative disorder in which tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-driven myofibroblast activity contributes to progressive digital flexion contractures by causing collagen deposition. Needle fasciotomy mechanically releases established collagen cords but does not target the underlying fibroproliferative process. Adalimumab, an anti-TNF agent, has been shown to reduce nodule hardness in early-stage Dupuytren disease, but it remains unknown whether it has additional impact combined with needle fasciotomy in more established contractures. QUESTIONS/PURPOSES: (1) Does a single perioperative intralesional injection of adalimumab immediately after needle fasciotomy increase the proportion of patients achieving at least 10° improvement in total passive extension deficit (TPED)? (2) Does adalimumab improve the change in TPED at 3 and 12 months? (3) Does adalimumab improve VAS pain and QuickDASH scores at 3 and 12 months? (4) What complications occurred in the adalimumab and placebo groups? METHODS: We conducted a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled pilot trial at a hand surgery department in a single academic center in adults with Dupuytren disease and an indication for needle fasciotomy. Eligible patients had a Dupuytren diathesis score greater than 4 and a nonfixed compound metacarpophalangeal and/or proximal interphalangeal contracture. Thirty patients were randomized 1:1 to receive a single 40-mg intralesional injection of adalimumab or matching saline placebo immediately after needle fasciotomy. One patient was excluded after randomization, leaving 29 patients for analysis (14 in the adalimumab group and 15 in the placebo). Fisher exact and Mann-Whitney U tests were used for categorical and continuous outcomes, respectively. RESULTS: Adalimumab did not improve the proportion of patients achieving at least a 10° improvement in TPED. At 3 months, 86% (12 of 14) of patients in the adalimumab group and 87% (13 of 15) in the placebo group achieved this improvement level, with a between-group difference in proportions of -1% (95% confidence interval [CI] -31% to 29%; p > 0.99). At 12 months, 71% (10 of 14) and 80% (12 of 15) of patients, respectively, achieved the endpoint, with a between-group difference of -9% (95% CI -41% to 24%; p = 0.68). Both groups showed no difference in change in TPED at 3 months; the median (IQR) change was -30° (-60° to -10°) versus -26° (-86° to -14°) at 3 months (Hodges-Lehmann estimate of between-group difference -4°; p = 0.76) and -32° (-60° to -5°) versus -24° (-80° to 5°) at 12 months (Hodges-Lehmann estimate of between-group difference 7°; p = 0.75). Pain and QuickDASH scores improved over time in both groups, with no between-group difference at 3 or 12 months (p > 0.05 for all). One procedure-related complication occurred; no adverse events related to either study injection were reported or observed. CONCLUSION: A single 40-mg intralesional injection of adalimumab added to needle fasciotomy did not improve extension, TPED, pain, or QuickDASH outcomes compared with placebo at 3 or 12 months. Given the absence of detected benefit in this pilot trial, adalimumab should not be used routinely as an adjunct to needle fasciotomy outside a clinical trial. Further studies investigating repeated or higher-dose regimens, treatment at earlier disease stages, and potential combination approaches are needed to better define the therapeutic role of anti-TNF treatment and determine whether it may have a clinical application before its use in routine practice can be considered. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: High-quality RCT from CORR comparing DAA versus posterolateral approach for THA, finding no meaningful difference in PROMs—directly challenges prevailing surgical trends with strong study design.
bullets: A single intralesional injection of adalimumab given immediately after needle fasciotomy did not improve finger extension, pain, or hand function compared to placebo at 3 or 12 months.
The finding applies to adults with established Dupuytren contracture and high diathesis scores undergoing needle fasciotomy.
Adalimumab should not be added to needle fasciotomy in routine practice until larger trials with repeated or higher doses clarify whether anti-TNF therapy has any role.

candidates.title: Height, Bone Quality, and Osteoarthritis Severity Predict Posterior Cruciate Ligament Footprint Injury Despite Using Robotic-Assisted Technology in Total Knee Arthroplasty.
candidates.authors_short: Leggieri F, Wood JA, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Robotic-assisted (RA) total knee arthroplasty (TKA) with haptic boundary protection allows preservation of posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) integrity to preserve native ligament function. This study aimed to identify pre- and intraoperative predictors of PCL footprint injury during RA cruciate-retaining TKA. METHODS: This prospective study analyzed 243 consecutive RA TKAs performed between January and August 2025. The PCL tibial footprint status was graded at the time of prosthetic implantation as intact or compromised. Data collection included demographics, preoperative alignment, osteoarthritis grading using International Cartilage Repair Society classification, bone quality assessment (5-point scale), and tibial resection thickness. The primary outcome was identification of independent factors predicting PCL footprint injury using multivariate logistic regressions. There were 26 patients (10.7%) who had a PCL footprint injury at the time of prosthetic implantation. RESULTS: There were five independent predictors that emerged from multivariate analyses (Chi-square = 35.0, Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) = 165.2, P = 0.014): poorest bone quality grade (odds ratio (OR) = 30.0, 95% confidence interval (CI): 2.5 to 360, P = 0.012); medial osteoarthritis severity (OR = 2.8, 95% CI: 1.2 to 6.5, P = 0.040); larger medial tibial cuts (OR = 2.2, 95% CI: 1.4 to 3.5, P = 0.010); lateral osteoarthritis severity (OR = 2.0, 95% CI: 1.4 to 2.9, P = 0.005); and patient height (OR = 0.9, 95% CI: 0.8 to 1.0, P = 0.023). A significant height × bone quality interaction was detected (Chi-square = 9.8; AIC = 158.5; P = 0.007; OR = 1.1; 95% CI: 1.05 to 1.3; P = 0.003). Significant differences between PCL-intact and PCL-compromised groups included medial tibial cut thickness (6.1 ± 1.3 versus 6.9 ± 0.9 mm, P = 0.001) and lateral osteoarthritis severity (2.4 ± 1.1 vs 3.0 ± 1.0, P = 0.005). CONCLUSION: Patients with shorter stature, poor bone quality, and advanced osteoarthritis are at increased risk for PCL footprint injury during RA TKA. With knowledge of these factors, development of preventative strategies to protect this critical structure is now required.
candidates.score_reasoning: Prospective double-blind RCT demonstrating a 79% reduction in opioid consumption with PENG block after THA, highly clinically relevant to perioperative pain management protocols.
bullets: PCL footprint injury occurred in 1 in 10 robotic-assisted cruciate-retaining TKAs despite haptic boundary protection.
Shorter patients with poor bone quality and advanced osteoarthritis on both compartments face the highest risk of PCL footprint damage during tibial resection.
Surgeons planning robotic cruciate-retaining TKA in this patient profile should consider modified resection strategies or have a posterior-stabilized implant available as a backup.

candidates.title: CORR Insights®: How Does the Achievement of Minimum Clinically Important Difference, Substantial Clinical Benefit, and Patient Acceptable Symptom State Change Over Time After Periacetabular Osteotomy?
candidates.score_reasoning: Large propensity-weighted retrospective cohort of 3,545 patients addressing timing of debridement in native joint septic arthritis, finding delayed surgery increases repeat debridement risk—highly actionable for emergency decision-making.
bullets: Periacetabular osteotomy outcomes improve progressively over time, with more patients reaching meaningful symptom thresholds at later follow-up points than at early postoperative visits.
These findings apply to younger patients with symptomatic hip dysplasia who are candidates for joint-preserving surgery before arthritis becomes advanced.
Surgeons should counsel patients that functional gains after periacetabular osteotomy continue beyond the early recovery period, so early dissatisfaction does not indicate failure.

candidates.title: Comparison of computed tomography-based tibial torsion measurement techniques reveals significant technique-dependent differences.
candidates.authors_short: Benefelds M, Juen U, et al.
candidates.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: To compare commonly used computed tomography (CT)-based tibial torsion measurement discrepancies and evaluate their intra- and interobserver agreement, as measurement discrepancies between techniques have not been systematically assessed. METHODS: CT scans from 20 adult patients were retrospectively analysed. Tibial torsion was calculated using two proximal reference axes (posterior tibial plateau tangent and tibial tuberosity axis) and four distal axes (transmalleolar, ankle joint, Jend and Waidelich). Three observers performed all measurements independently and repeated them after 8-12 weeks. Differences among techniques were assessed using repeated-measures analysis of variance with Bonferroni correction. Reliability was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). RESULTS: All measurement techniques differed significantly (p < 0.05). Mean tibial torsion was 34.1° (standard deviation [SD] 8.6°) for the transmalleolar axis, 31.2° (SD 8.8°) for the ankle joint axis, 44.2° (SD 9.8°) for the Jend axis and 34.9° (SD 9.0°) for the Waidelich axis. Segmental values revealed a mean supratuberositary torsion of 26° (SD 6.7°) and a mean infratuberositary torsion of 7.9° (SD 8.8°) for the transmalleolar axis, 5.1° (SD 8.9°) for the ankle joint axis, 18.1° (SD 10.4°) for the Jend axis and 8.8° (SD 9.1°) for the Waidelich axis. All techniques showed excellent intra- and interobserver reliability (ICC > 0.89). CONCLUSION: Tibial torsion values depended strongly on the measurement technique used. Technique-specific normative values are essential, and radiology reports should explicitly identify the technique applied. Clinicians must account for these systematic differences when interpreting torsion values and planning derotational osteotomies. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective comparative study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Long-term 20-year cohort showing combined coronal and rotational malalignment in TKA is an independent predictor of aseptic revision with 88.3% survivorship versus 97.2%, adding novel rotational alignment insight to alignment literature.
bullets: CT-based tibial torsion measurements vary by up to 13 degrees depending on which proximal and distal reference axes are used, even when reliability is excellent across all techniques.
These differences apply to any patient undergoing torsion assessment for derotational osteotomy planning, where choosing the wrong reference can meaningfully alter surgical targets.

Surgeons should confirm which measurement technique was used before interpreting a torsion value, and institutions should adopt technique-specific normative ranges rather than a single universal threshold.

candidates.title: Outcomes associated with suprapectoral versus subpectoral biceps tenodesis site after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair: a retrospective comparative cohort analysis.
candidates.authors_short: Rosso C, Loske S, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To investigate functional outcomes, groove pain, presence of Popeye sign and complications associated with suprapectoral and subpectoral biceps tenodesis site in rotator cuff (RC) surgery. METHODS: Within the ARCR_Pred multicenter cohort study, patients from 19 centers undergoing primary arthroscopic RC repair between June 2020 and November 2021 were prospectively enrolled. Patients undergoing biceps tenodesis without preoperative Popeye sign were allocated to suprapectoral or subpectoral groups, respectively. Outcomes (range of motion, pain, strength, Subjective Shoulder Value, Constant-Murley Score, Oxford Shoulder Score, quality of life (EQ-5D-5L), groove pain, Popeye sign, Speed's test, and postoperative adverse events) were compared using adjusted mixed models. Propensity-score matching was performed as a sensitivity analysis. RESULTS: Among 445 eligible patients (242 suprapectoral, 203 subpectoral), biceps-specific outcomes were not significantly different for all parameters except for postoperative Popeye sign, being more frequent in the suprapectoral group (36 (15%) vs. 10 (5%); Odds ratio [OR] 0.20; P = 0.009). Shoulder abduction strength at 90° was higher in the suprapectoral cohort at 12 months postoperatively (7.1 vs. 6.3 kg; adjusted difference 0.8; P = 0.024), not reaching minimal clinical important difference. All other functional outcome parameters demonstrated no clinically significant differences. Biceps specific complications were not significantly different between groups. The propensity-score matching sensitivity analysis supported these findings except for the shoulder abduction strength. CONCLUSION: Suprapectoral tenodesis was associated with a higher prevalence of postoperative Popeye sign. No significant differences were detected in postoperative groove pain. The observed strength advantage after suprapectoral tenodesis was not clinically meaningful. Procedure-specific complication rates were low in both groups.
candidates.score_reasoning: Comparative study of 774 THAs showing triple-taper metaphyseal stems have 5-fold lower periprosthetic fracture risk than other cementless designs, directly influencing implant selection decisions.
bullets: In patients undergoing biceps tenodesis during rotator cuff repair, suprapectoral fixation produced a Popeye deformity three times more often than subpectoral fixation (15% vs. 5%).
Groove pain, functional scores, and complication rates were equivalent between suprapectoral and subpectoral tenodesis sites across 445 patients.

For surgeons counseling patients before rotator cuff repair with tenodesis, subpectoral fixation significantly reduces the cosmetic risk of a Popeye deformity without sacrificing any functional outcome.

candidates.title: Functional outcomes over 24 months after arthroscopic repair of isolated subscapularis tendon tears in a multicentre study.
candidates.authors_short: Audigé L, Croci E, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Isolated subscapularis tears are rare, and it is currently unclear how the tear size relates to the postoperative outcomes after arthroscopic repair. This study aimed to evaluate clinical- and patient-reported outcomes, as well as adverse events of arthroscopically treated isolated subscapularis tears based on the tear extent over 24 months. METHODS: Across 19 orthopaedic centres, 69 patients undergoing primary arthroscopic repair for isolated subscapularis tears were prospectively recruited between June 2020 and November 2021. Medical imaging examinations were conducted at baseline and at 12 months. Clinical- and patient-reported outcomes were obtained at baseline, 6, 12, and 24 months. Adverse events within 24 months were documented. Patients were grouped into partial tears (n = 14), full-thickness tears of the superior half (n = 35) or complete full-thickness tears (n = 20) of the subscapularis. All outcomes were compared using generalised linear mixed models adjusted for baseline values, age, sex, American Society of Anaesthesiologists classification, tear aetiology, and steroid infiltrations. RESULTS: Improvements in all outcome scores were observed after surgery. No group differences were observed in the ranges of motion in flexion, abduction and external rotation (P≥0.634). The partial tear group had a higher pain level than both full-thickness groups at 12 months (P≤0.005). Abduction strength, Constant Score, Oxford Shoulder Score, Subjective Shoulder Value and EQ-5D-5L showed positive changes within 12- or 24-month follow-ups, with no group differences (P≥0.089). The risk of at least a symptomatic adverse event of any severity level affecting the operated shoulder and arm was highest for patients with partial tears (50%) and lowest for patients with complete full-thickness tears (25%). The most frequent occurrences were persistent or worsening pain, stiffness, and recurrent defects. Overall, 62% of patients with partial tears, 97% of patients with superior full-thickness tears and 77% of patients with complete full-thickness tears were satisfied at 24 months. CONCLUSION: Arthroscopic repair of isolated subscapularis tears leads to significant and sustained improvements in clinical and patient-reported outcomes over 24 months, regardless of tear extent. However, patients with partial tears demonstrated greater residual pain and fewer patients reported satisfaction compared with those with full-thickness tears. These findings may reflect differences in patient characteristics and surgical treatment choices. Further studies are needed to determine the suitability and efficacy of surgical treatments for isolated subscapularis partial tears. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, Retrospective Cohort Comparison, Prognosis Study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Registry study of 1,683 shoulders showing low glenohumeral radial mismatch is associated with higher revision for aseptic loosening, providing implant selection guidance for anatomic TSA.
bullets: Arthroscopic repair of isolated subscapularis tears improves strength, range of motion, and patient-reported scores by 24 months regardless of whether the tear is partial or full-thickness.
Patients with partial subscapularis tears report more residual pain and lower satisfaction at 24 months compared to those with full-thickness tears, despite similar functional gains.
Surgeons should counsel patients with partial subscapularis tears that outcomes are less predictable, and further evidence is needed before surgery becomes the default treatment for this group.

candidates.title: Clinical Outcomes of Three-Dimensional Printed Implants in Bone Tumor Surgery: A Meta-Analysis.
candidates.authors_short: Qureshi S, Kralovich A, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: The advent of three-dimensional (3D) printing has helped to revolutionize the field of orthopaedic surgery, particularly in the realm of preoperative planning and education. Another application of 3D printing in orthopaedic surgery is the production of patient-specific prostheses for reconstruction. The goal of this study was to analyze the use of 3D-printed prostheses in the setting of orthopaedic oncologic surgical resection and reconstruction. METHODS: A systematic meta-analysis was conducted using data from previous trials comparing 3D-printed prostheses (3DPs) with historical reconstruction across multiple anatomic locations, including the spine, pelvis, and extremities, in musculoskeletal oncology. Key outcomes assessed were surgical duration, intraoperative blood loss, complication rates, dislocation rates, resection accuracy, and functional outcomes using Musculoskeletal Tumor Society scores. RESULTS: A total of eight studies involving 237 patients (113 in the 3D-printed prosthesis group and 124 in the control group) were included. Compared with historical reconstruction, 3DP use showed a significant reduction in surgical duration (mean difference -37.6 minutes; 95% confidence interval [CI], -59.3 to -15.8; P = 0.0007) and postoperative complications (Odds Ratio [OR], 0.20; 95% CI, 0.07 to 0.59; P = 0.0038). The 3DP group also demonstrated significantly lower recurrence (OR, 0.34; 95% CI, 0.13 to 0.88; P = 0.026) and higher resection accuracy in the subset of studies reporting this outcome (OR, 14.36; 95% CI, 2.22 to 92.64; P = 0.0051). Functional outcomes improved with 3DP reconstruction, with a higher Musculoskeletal Tumor Society score (mean difference +3.78; 95% CI, 2.09 to 5.48; P < 0.001). CONCLUSION: Patient-specific 3D-printed protheses were associated with improved functional outcomes and favorable perioperative and oncologic end points, including shorter surgical time, fewer complications, and lower recurrence. These findings emphasize the value of 3DP technology in enhancing patient outcomes; however, owing to substantial heterogeneity and limited study volume, additional high-quality, randomized studies are needed to validate its broader clinical influence.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large multi-institutional study showing ALIF carries 2-fold higher VTE risk than TLIF at all time points, directly informing perioperative thromboprophylaxis protocols for spine surgeons.
bullets: In 237 patients undergoing bone tumor resection and reconstruction, custom 3D-printed implants reduced operative time by nearly 38 minutes and cut complication rates by 80% compared to standard reconstruction.
Patients with spine, pelvis, or extremity tumors reconstructed with 3D-printed implants had lower local recurrence rates and higher resection accuracy than those treated with conventional prostheses.

For orthopaedic oncology surgeons, these findings support considering patient-specific 3D-printed implants as a viable reconstruction option, though the evidence base remains small and randomized trials are still needed.

candidates.title: Clinical predictors of lateral meniscal hypermobility and development of the Hypermobile Lateral Meniscus Syndrome Score.
candidates.authors_short: Endara Urresta F, Barros Castro A, Peñaherrera-Carrillo C
candidates.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: To identify independent preoperative predictors of arthroscopically confirmed lateral meniscal hypermobility and to develop and internally validate the Hypermobile Lateral Meniscus Syndrome Score (HLMSS). METHODS: A retrospective diagnostic prediction model study included 482 patients undergoing knee arthroscopy: 156 with lateral meniscal hypermobility, 171 with structural lateral meniscal tears without hypermobility and 155 arthroscopic controls. Lateral meniscal hypermobility was defined arthroscopically as reproducible anterior translation of the posterior horn beyond the midpoint (>50%) of the lateral tibial plateau. Preoperative clinical and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) variables were evaluated as candidate predictors. Independent predictors were identified using multivariable logistic regression, and the HLMSS was derived from regression coefficients. Internal validation was performed using 1000 bootstrap resamples. Discrimination, calibration and clinical utility were assessed. RESULTS: The cohort included 482 patients (mean age, 31.8 ± 9.4 years; 62.4% male). Mean age was 28.9 ± 8.1 years in the hypermobility group, 34.7 ± 10.2 years in the structural tear group, and 31.8 ± 8.7 years in controls; 64.7%, 60.8% and 61.9% were male, respectively. Independent predictors of lateral meniscal hypermobility were intermittent locking (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 4.78), hyperflexion pain (aOR, 4.21), rotational instability sensation (aOR, 3.74), posterolateral pain (aOR, 3.12) and popliteomeniscal fascicle abnormality on MRI (aOR, 2.68). The HLMSS demonstrated an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.91 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.88-0.94) and an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.89. At ≥7 points, sensitivity was 86.5% and specificity was 84.8%. In the restricted comparison with structural lateral meniscal tears, the AUC was 0.84 (95% CI, 0.80-0.88). CONCLUSION: The HLMSS demonstrated good to excellent discrimination for identifying arthroscopically confirmed lateral meniscal hypermobility using preoperative clinical and MRI findings. External validation in consecutive symptomatic populations is required before routine clinical implementation. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective diagnostic cohort study.
candidates.score_reasoning: RCT of 96 patients showing extended perioperative duloxetine does not reduce chronic postsurgical pain incidence after THA, providing a negative but important finding for pain prevention strategies.
bullets: Five preoperative findings predict lateral meniscal hypermobility at arthroscopy: intermittent locking, hyperflexion pain, rotational instability, posterolateral pain, and popliteomeniscal fascicle abnormality on MRI.

Combining these findings into the HLMSS score, a threshold of 7 or more points identified hypermobility with 87% sensitivity and 85% specificity in patients under 35 presenting with lateral knee symptoms.

Surgeons evaluating young patients with lateral knee locking and hyperflexion pain can use this clinical score to raise suspicion for meniscal hypermobility before arthroscopy, though external validation is still needed.

candidates.title: Effect of Mechanical Alignment on Clinically Significant Outcomes, Reoperation, and Failure After Osteochondral Allograft Transplantation of the Knee.
candidates.authors_short: Sardesai KS, Ackermann J, et al.
candidates.journal: The American journal of sports medicine
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Identifying and addressing mechanical malalignment is an important component of treating symptomatic osteochondral defects with osteochondral allograft (OCA) transplantation. However, little is known about how malalignment influences short- to midterm outcomes after OCA transplantation. PURPOSE: To evaluate whether mechanical alignment measurements including the hip-knee-ankle (HKA) angle, lateral distal femoral angle (LDFA), medial proximal tibial angle (MPTA), and joint line convergence angle (JLCA) predict clinically significant outcome achievement, graft failure, and reoperation after OCA transplantation with or without concomitant realignment. STUDY DESIGN: Case series; Level of evidence, 4. METHODS: Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) were collected preoperatively and at a minimum 2-year follow-up in patients receiving OCA from 2005 to 2023. PROMs included the International Knee Documentation Committee score and Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score subscales. Clinically significant outcome thresholds were the minimal clinically important difference (MCID), substantial clinical benefit (SCB), and Patient Acceptable Symptom State (PASS). Preoperative full-length, weightbearing radiographs were used to measure the HKA angle, LDFA, MPTA, and JLCA. Multivariable logistic regression was used for clinically significant outcome achievement and all-cause reoperation; failure and arthroplasty were summarized descriptively because of the low number of events. RESULTS: A total of 66 patients (mean age, 34.1 ± 11.5 years; mean body mass index, 27.8 ± 4.8 kg/m2; 50% female) met inclusion criteria. Mean alignment measurements were 1.8°± 4.0° for the HKA angle, 86.8°± 2.3° for the LDFA, 86.3°± 2.3° for the MPTA, and 1.7°± 1.0° for the JLCA. Although PROMs improved at the final follow-up, no preoperative alignment measure was statistically associated with MCID, PASS, or SCB achievement or with all-cause reoperation (P > .05). In total, 25 (37.9%) patients underwent reoperation; graft survivorship was 93.9%, with 4 failures and 3 arthroplasty conversions. In an exploratory subanalysis, 16 patients with an HKA angle >5° of varus or valgus (13 with concomitant realignment) did not have significantly different rates of reoperation (43.8% vs 36.0%; P = .768) or graft failure (6.3% vs 6.0%; P > .999) compared to their remaining counterparts. CONCLUSION: In this small, heterogeneous cohort, preoperative mechanical alignment measures were not statistically associated with clinically significant outcome achievement or all-cause reoperation after OCA transplantation. These hypothesis-generating findings do not establish the absence of an alignment effect or define a threshold for realignment because most patients with severe preoperative malalignment underwent concomitant realignment, which may have contributed to the favorable overall outcomes, and failure events were infrequent.
candidates.score_reasoning: Meta-analysis showing 3D-printed prostheses in oncologic surgery reduce operative time by 38 minutes and complication rates 5-fold, with meaningful implications for orthopaedic oncology reconstruction planning.
bullets: In 66 patients undergoing osteochondral allograft transplantation of the knee, preoperative alignment measurements did not predict which patients achieved meaningful pain and function improvements at two-year follow-up.
Patients with significant varus or valgus deformity greater than 5 degrees who underwent concomitant realignment had similar reoperation and graft failure rates compared to well-aligned patients.

Graft survivorship was 94 percent overall, suggesting that correcting malalignment at the time of grafting may preserve outcomes, though this study was too small to define a firm realignment threshold.
